title: Marketing Loops: Corey Haines's playbook for recurring, agent-run marketing workflows
summary: Corey's open-source "marketing-loops" skill defines how to turn manual marketing tasks into repeatable agent-run workflows on a cadence. Each loop needs nine parts, including a self-check, state handling and a stop condition. The skill stresses matching cadence to signal speed, keeping humans on spend and publish actions, and adopting loops one at a time.

principles.text: Match a loop's cadence to how fast the signal changes, not how often you want updates.
principles.quote: Match cadence to how fast the signal actually changes — not to how often you'd *like* an update.

principles.text: Over-frequent loops are the most common failure: busywork, burned budget, ignored output.
principles.quote: Over-frequent loops are the most common failure mode: they generate busywork, burn budget, and train you to ignore the output.

principles.text: Separate how often a loop checks from when it acts; most runs should be "checked, nothing to do."
principles.quote: Most runs of a good loop are "checked, nothing to do."

principles.text: Let agents draft freely, but gate publishing and budget shifts behind a human unless explicitly authorized with caps.
principles.quote: Auto-*drafting* an ad, email, or post is fine. Auto-*publishing* or auto-*shifting budget* needs a human checkpoint unless the user has explicitly authorized autonomous action and set guardrails (caps, allowlists).

principles.text: Every loop needs a self-check before acting, so it doesn't react to noise, seasonality or tracking bugs.
principles.quote: No self-check → the loop acts on noise, seasonality, or a tracking bug.

principles.text: Delete vanity loops that nobody acts on, and build one loop at a time instead of ten at once.
principles.quote: If nobody acts on the output, delete the loop. A loop that emails a dashboard nobody reads is worse than nothing.
